hook.text: Yeast makes ethanol from corn — but engineering bacteria to make butanol or biodiesel could replace petroleum.

buildup.text: Cellulosic ethanol breaks down wood and straw — enzymes from termite gut microbes digest the tough cellulose.

discovery.text: Engineered E. coli produces fatty acid ethyl esters — molecules chemically identical to diesel fuel.

twist.text: Biofuels struggle on cost — petroleum is still cheaper, and scaling fermentation is capital-intensive.

climax.text: Algae bioreactors produce lipids at 10 times the yield of soy per acre — but harvesting costs remain high.

punchline.text: Microbes that brew fuel — biofuels turn sugar into energy independence.

quiz.question: Why haven't biofuels replaced petroleum despite technical success?
options: Biofuels produce fewer BTUs than petroleum fuels
Production costs and scaling challenges make biofuels more expensive than petroleum
Biofuels cannot be used in existing engines without modification

details.summary: Synthetic biology engineers microorganisms to produce fuels like ethanol, butanol, biodiesel, and even jet fuel from renewable biomass. Engineered algae and bacteria convert sunlight or plant sugars into hydrocarbons that can directly replace fossil fuels in existing infrastructure.
details.whyItMatters: Transportation accounts for a quarter of global carbon emissions. Biofuels produced by engineered organisms offer a carbon-neutral alternative that can use existing engines and distribution networks without requiring new infrastructure.
takeaways: Engineered microbes produce ethanol, butanol, and hydrocarbon fuels from biomass
Algae can convert sunlight and CO2 directly into biodiesel precursors
Drop-in biofuels are chemically identical to petroleum fuels

faq.question: How do engineered organisms produce transportation fuels?
faq.answer: Yeast and bacteria are engineered with metabolic pathways that convert sugars from corn, sugarcane, or cellulose into ethanol or higher alcohols. Algae use photosynthesis to make lipids convertible to biodiesel. Some engineered E. coli produce hydrocarbons identical to gasoline.

faq.question: Why have biofuels not replaced fossil fuels despite decades of development?
faq.answer: Economics remain the primary challenge. Low petroleum prices make biofuels uncompetitive without subsidies. Cellulosic ethanol processing is expensive. Algal biofuels face scaling difficulties. Food versus fuel competition for cropland raises sustainability questions about corn ethanol.
